mainEntity.name: How should I answer why should we hire you?

acceptedAnswer.text: Name a need in the role, give a specific example showing you can help with it, and connect that experience to the work ahead. Use evidence from your own background rather than claiming to be better than candidates you have not met.

mainEntity.name: How do I answer why should we hire you with no experience?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use relevant evidence from coursework, volunteering, personal projects, or part-time work. Explain what you contributed and learned, then be clear about which parts of the job you are ready to do and where you would need support.

mainEntity.name: How long should a why should we hire you answer be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Aim for roughly a minute as a practice target, not a strict rule. One or two relevant examples are usually enough to start the conversation. Leave room for the interviewer to ask for details.

mainEntity.name: Is why should we hire you the same as tell me about yourself?

acceptedAnswer.text: They overlap, but the emphasis differs. Tell me about yourself introduces the relevant parts of your background. Why should we hire you asks you to connect your evidence more directly to what this particular role needs.

h1: Why Should We Hire You? A Clear Answer with 4 Examples
lead: Build a convincing answer to why should we hire you using the job requirements and your real experience, with examples for graduates and experienced candidates.
author: Amigo Team

hero.alt: A candidate explaining her experience to an interviewer across a meeting table.

html:
Answer “Why should we hire you?” by connecting a real need in the job to something you have already done. Explain the evidence, then say how it would help you contribute. You can be confident without claiming to be the best person in the applicant pool.

The question can feel awkward. You have already discussed your resume, and now you are being asked to make the case again. The useful move is to bring the conversation back to the employer's problem: what needs doing, and what makes you equipped to help?

Harvard's interviewing guide describes this question as an underlying concern across an interview: employers want to understand the connection between your skills, interests, and the position. Our answer structure below is a practical way to make that connection explicit.

Build the answer from the job, not a list of adjectives

Start with one important requirement. “Good communicator” is broad. “Explain technical incidents to customer-facing teams” gives you a more useful target.

Next, choose a real example. You might have written incident updates, taught a difficult concept, or helped a support team understand a recurring error. Explain what you did and what changed. A precise outcome does not always require a percentage; a team adopting your troubleshooting guide is an observable result.

Finally, connect the example to the role. Do not make the interviewer do all the translation. “That experience would help me keep support and engineering aligned during the incidents you described” completes the thought.

The outline is simple:

  • Need: “You mentioned that this role will…”
  • Evidence: “In my last project, I…”
  • Connection: “That would help me contribute by…”

Use those as notes rather than repeating the exact phrasing. Your answer should sound like part of the conversation you are already having.

Example 1: A recent graduate

The following examples are fictional illustrations. Adapt the structure to your own history; the experience and results are not claims about real candidates.

“This role needs someone who can investigate data problems and explain what they find. In my final-year project, I checked the source data before we built the dashboard and found that two files used different definitions of an active customer. I documented the difference, agreed a definition with the project supervisor, and updated our analysis. I have not worked with your production systems yet, but I can bring that habit of checking assumptions and making my work understandable.”

This answer does not apologize for being a graduate. It offers evidence at an appropriate level and acknowledges a real learning gap.

Example 2: An experienced software engineer

“You said the team needs to make the service easier to operate while continuing to deliver product work. In my current role, I took ownership of a recurring support issue, added logging around the failing path, and worked with support to write a diagnosis guide. Other engineers could then investigate the issue without waiting for me. That experience is relevant to the operational work you described, and I would want to understand your current incident patterns before proposing changes.”

Notice the balance between relevance and restraint. The candidate does not promise to fix an unfamiliar system in the first week.

Example 3: A career changer

“My background is in customer support, and I am moving into customer success. The part that transfers most directly is helping customers get past recurring obstacles. I have led onboarding calls, documented where customers got stuck, and worked with our product team to improve the setup instructions. I would need to learn your account-planning process, but I already have experience turning a customer conversation into a clear next step and following through.”

For a career change, explain the transfer. A title alone may not show why your experience matters. Our opening-answer guide can help you make the same transition clear at the start of an interview.

Example 4: A team lead

“From our conversation, the team needs clearer priorities across several projects. In my last role, I introduced a weekly review where we made dependencies visible and agreed which requests would wait. I also worked with the other leads to make sure individual engineers were not being given conflicting commitments. That is the kind of coordination I could bring here, while learning where your current planning process already works well.”

The answer names a mechanism, not just a leadership trait. Be prepared for the follow-up: “What happened when another lead disagreed?” If you cannot explain the story beyond the prepared summary, choose a different example.

What weakens an otherwise good answer?

A string of claims without evidence. “I am motivated, adaptable, and hardworking” leaves the interviewer to guess what those qualities look like. Keep one claim and show it.

An answer about what you need alone. Wanting growth, stability, or a new challenge is reasonable. This particular answer also needs to explain what you bring to the work.

Comparing yourself with unknown candidates. You can describe your strengths without saying nobody else has them. “My combination of support and engineering experience is relevant here” is easier to support than “I am your strongest candidate.”

Promising a result you cannot control. You do not yet know every constraint. Describe the experience and approach you bring instead of inventing a first-quarter impact target.

Practice the follow-up, too

Say the answer aloud, then ask yourself three questions: What did I personally do? How do I know it helped? What would I do differently now? If you are short on evidence, revise the claim rather than adding impressive language.

Use the job description as your starting point, then update the answer with what you learn in the interview. If the manager has spent ten minutes explaining a handoff problem, a relevant example about handoffs may be more helpful than the answer you prepared about speed.

For more practice choosing evidence, read our behavioral interview guide. The aim is a concise explanation you can discuss, not a speech you can only deliver from the beginning.
